record.title: The zero coefficient is not minimizing

aligned_passages.text: **Theorem 5.1 (full support).** In the pure zero-field SK model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimize $\mathcal P$. Then $\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing. For every associated diffusion started at zero, $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for $0\le t<1$. Keep the same minimiser, diffusion and moment function $q$ throughout. Section 3 has established $G\ge0$, $G=0$ on the support $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$, and the contact conditions $q(s)=s$, $q'(s)\le1$ at support points. At zero, the value identity comes from symmetry, and the slope bound requires $0\in S$. Section 4 supplies curvature on constant intervals for every admissible coefficient. These premises are available before any support gap is excluded. We first deal with the endpoint at one, then use the curvature estimate on the remaining intervals. For a terminal interval $(a,1)$, including empty support $[0,1)$, the cusp estimate gives $1-q(t)\gtrsim\sqrt{1-t}$ and hence $G<0$ near one. On a positive plateau with two contact endpoints, strict convexity puts $q'$ below its endpoint chord, although its integral must equal the interval length. On a zero plateau the heat argument makes $q'$ strictly increasing, below the right contact slope. At an initial gap, use the one-sided contact slope if $0\in S$; otherwise the coefficient is zero and symmetry supplies $q(0)=0$. **Why a terminal plateau violates the variational inequality.** Suppose that $\gamma=c$ on $(a,1)$, where $0\le a<1$ and $c\ge0$ is finite. The endpoint $1$ is outside the support domain, so there is no contact condition there to complete an endpoint-chord argument. Instead we will prove $$ 1-q(t)\ge C\sqrt{1-t} \tag{5.1} $$ for some $C>0$ and every $t$ sufficiently close to one. The proof separates two facts: the diffusion puts positive probability density near zero, and the smoothed terminal slope has a definite deficit from $\pm1$ in a shrinking window around zero. Fix $s\in(a,1)$ and let $\rho_s$ be the law of $X_s$. Choose $R<\infty$ such that $p_0=\rho_s([-R,R])>0$. For $c>0$, set $$ h(t,y)=\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt{1-t}Z|},\qquad \Phi(t,y)=c^{-1}\log h(t,y), $$ where $Z$ is standard normal. The drift on this interval is $c\Phi_x=h_x/h$, and the transition density is $$ k_{s,t}(x,y)=p_{t-s}(y-x)\frac{h(t,y)}{h(s,x)},\qquad p_v(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2v)}. \tag{5.2} $$ The heat-semigroup identity normalises this kernel; equivalently, for Brownian motion started at $(s,x)$, $h(t,B_t)/h(s,x)$ is the positive mean-one change of measure which adds the drift $h_x/h$. For $c=0$, the same kernel formula applies with $h=1$, and the value function is the ordinary heat evolution of $|x|$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, proof of (6.6)][fs-var]. Put $L=1-s$ and $\delta=L/2$. For $s+\delta\le t<1$, $|x|\le R$ and $|y|\le1$, $$ p_{t-s}(y-x)\ge (2\pi L)^{-1/2}e^{-(R+1)^2/(2\delta)}=:k_*>0, $$ while $h(t,y)\ge1$ and $h(s,x)\le e^{cR}\mathbb E e^{c\sqrt L|Z|}=:M<\infty$. Integrating (5.2) over the part of $\rho_s$ in $[-R,R]$ therefore gives a density $f_t$ of $X_t$ with $$ f_t(y)\ge p_0k_*/M=:m>0 \quad(s+\delta\le t<1,\ |y|\le1). \tag{5.3} $$ Only positive mass of a compact set was needed at time $s$; no density assumption on $\rho_s$ has entered. Now write $\varepsilon=1-t$ and restrict to $|y|\le\sqrt\varepsilon$. Differentiating the terminal heat formula gives, with the unweighted interpretation for $c=0$, $$ u(t,y)= \frac{\mathbb E[\operatorname{sgn}(y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z) e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}]} {\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}}. $$ The denominator is at most $D=e^c\mathbb E e^{c|Z|}<\infty$. Each sign has unnormalised mass at least $p_*:=\mathbb P(Z\ge1)>0$: the threshold $|y/\sqrt\varepsilon|$ is at most one, and the exponential weight is at least one. Hence each sign has tilted probability at least $\theta=p_*/D\in(0,1/2)$. It follows that $$ |u(t,y)|\le1-2\theta,\qquad 1-u(t,y)^2\ge4\theta(1-\theta)=:\kappa>0. $$ Multiplying this uniform deficit by the density lower bound (5.3) and the window width $2\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,y)^2)f_t(y)\,dy \ge 2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ This proves (5.1) with $C=2m\kappa$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, density and terminal-window estimates][fs-var]. The sign of the contradiction is now explicit. For $s'$ sufficiently close to one, the estimate holds at every $t\in[s',1)$, so $$ \begin{aligned} G(s')&=\int_{s'}^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\\ &\le\frac{(1-s')^2}{2} -\frac{2C}{3}(1-s')^{3/2}<0. \end{aligned} $$ The final inequality holds once $\sqrt{1-s'}<4C/3$. It contradicts the nonnegative cost of adding an atom at $s'$. This proof covers $c=0$ as well as $c>0$. In particular, empty support is impossible: then $\mu_\gamma=0$ and $\gamma=0$ on all of $[0,1)$. The terminal-plateau conclusion was already recorded in [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Remark 7][acz]; the estimates above supply the quantitative argument needed here. **A shorter qualitative exclusion.** The existing curvature input also excludes a terminal support gap without estimating its boundary layer. Here is the elementary calculus step. Suppose $q\in C^1([r,1))$, $q(r)=r$, $q'(r)\le1$, $q\le1$, and $q'$ is strictly convex on $(r,1)$. If $q(t)\ge t$ at some $r1$. Compact-strip regularity gives continuity of $q'$ on $[a,b]$, even if $\gamma$ jumps at an endpoint. Contact gives $$ q(a)=a,\qquad q(b)=b,\qquad q'(a),q'(b)\le1. \tag{5.4} $$ If the constant coefficient is $c>0$, Section 4 makes $q'$ strictly convex in the gap. Continuity extends the chord comparison to its endpoints, giving $$ q'(t)<\frac{b-t}{b-a}q'(a)+\frac{t-a}{b-a}q'(b)\le1, \qquad a0. $$ The first term is nonnegative; strict convexity makes the second positive. Only continuity of $q'$ is needed at the ends. For example, a jump $\Delta\gamma$ at $s$ gives the one-sided identity $$ q''(s+)-q''(s-)=-2\Delta\gamma\,\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^3. $$ It follows by applying Itô's formula to $a^2$ and using continuity of its derivative moments on a compact strip. Taking $\gamma=0$ before $s=1/2$ and $\gamma=1/2$ afterward makes this jump strictly negative; the terminal Cole–Hopf solution has positive Hessian. Thus continuity of $q'$ does not license classical higher time derivatives across coefficient jumps. [OpenAI (2026a), proof of Corollary 6.4][fs-density]. If $(0,b)$ is a gap and $0\in S$, the preceding proof applies using the one-sided contact slope bound at zero. Because $(0,b)$ contains no mass, the support condition at zero forces an atom there and hence $c=\gamma(0)>0$. Its absence has not been proved at this stage. If instead the complementary component is $[0,b)$ with $0\notin S$, there is no mass anywhere in $[0,b)$. Thus $\gamma=0$ there. The identity $q(0)=0$ comes from zero-field symmetry, and the right endpoint gives $q(b)=b$, $q'(b)\le1$. Here $q''(t)>0$ for $00 \qquad(0\le a0$ is already impossible: either $h\le1$ everywhere, forcing $h\equiv1$ by its integral, or it attains an interior maximum above one, where $h'=0$ and $h''\le0$. This is an elementary deduction from these premises. Chen's conditional crossing theorem, with its own hypotheses, is of this form; §4 proves the stronger $q'''>0$ throughout a positive plateau, without a minimizer premise. See [Chen, arXiv:2607.18032v1, Proposition 4.2 and the proof of Proposition 4.3][chen26]. Neither statement supplies terminal contact at the excluded endpoint one.

### 10.3 The zero coefficient The admissible coefficient $\gamma_0=0$ makes the use of minimality in the normalization step explicit. Its diffusion is $X_t=B_t$, and the [zero-coefficient heat formula][fs-reg] gives $$ u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1, \qquad a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}}{\sqrt{1-t}}. $$ Since $\mathbb E e^{-\lambda B_t^2}=(1+2\lambda t)^{-1/2}$, $$ \mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi},\qquad \mathbb E a_0(t,B_t)^2=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t. $$ The last identity follows by integrating $q_0'=\mathbb E a_0^2$ from $q_0(0)=0$. This heat and late-step variation argument is the zero-field specialization of [Chen, Handschy and Lerman, Theorem 6 and its proof, arXiv:1609.04368v4, pp. 13–16](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4). The Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model asks us to choose signs that
maximise a random sum of pair interactions. The Parisi formula expresses
the limiting maximum through a nondecreasing function, the **order
parameter**. We explain why a minimising order parameter cannot be
constant on any interval below one.

The proof compares two consequences of a hypothetical gap. Minimality
fixes the values and bounds the slopes of an auxiliary curve at its
endpoints. An analytic estimate makes the derivative strictly convex
between them, leaving too little area to connect the required values.
Initial and terminal gaps need separate arguments. We then return to
the spins: a theorem about their energies gives nearly optimal sign
choices differing on any prescribed positive fraction of positions up to one half,
with arbitrarily small error in that fraction.

We follow the quantitative proof in [OpenAI (2026a)][support-manuscript];
[Hong-Bin Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3][chen-support] had already proved
full support by a different method. The estimate used here makes the
final contradiction a direct comparison of areas. We assume algebra
and elementary calculus, and introduce probability and cumulative mass
through calculations. The deeper analytic facts are stated where the
proof needs them. By the end of Sections 1–6, the reader should be able
to reconstruct how minimality and those inputs exclude each kind of gap,
then translate the result into a statement about spin configurations.
Section 7 gives optional calculations and answers to the short questions
in the text; the full analytic proofs remain in the cited sources.

## 4. The full-support theorem

**Source theorem ([OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][support-manuscript]).**
In the pure, zero-field model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma$ be an
admissible integrable minimiser of $\mathcal P$. Its Stieltjes measure
has full relative support on $[0,1)$, and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing.
For every associated diffusion and every $0\le t<1$,

$$
\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]=t,\qquad
\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1.
$$

The cumulative function determines its measure uniquely; for a fixed
Brownian motion the associated diffusion is unique by the cited
regularity results. The theorem requires a minimiser,
not merely an admissible candidate. Zero field supplies $q(0)=0$;
$\xi''=1$ enters the curvature estimate. The statement does not cover
nonzero field or general mixed-spin covariance functions.

### 5.4 The remaining initial and terminal gaps **Initial gap with zero outside the support.** Suppose $[0,s)$ is missing and $s<1$ is the first support point. Then $\gamma=0$ there, so the positive-coefficient bound supplies no strictness. Instead the zero-coefficient heat identity gives $$ q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0\qquad(00$. To control a later slope, use the same chord rule on the larger interval $[r,s]$, where $t0. $$ Consequently $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))$. Choose any time $$ t+\frac{1-t}{1+h(t)}0$, and the lower bound now gives $q(s)>1$, contradicting $q(s)\le1$ strictly before time one. Thus $q(t)[§5, terminal estimate](../long/reasoning-record.md#terminal-gap). [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Remark 7][acz] had already recorded the absence of terminal plateaus. These cases exhaust the complement of the support. Contact now gives $q(t)=t$ for every interior time, and symmetry includes zero. Differentiating gives $\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1$, completing the theorem.

### 7.1 Why the zero candidate does not minimise

Return to the Gaussian value and slope from Section 3. With $\gamma=0$,
the state is $B_t$. Differentiating the slope once more gives

$$
X_t=B_t,\qquad
u_0(t,x)=2F_{\mathrm G}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right)-1,
\qquad
a_0(t,x)=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi(1-t)}}e^{-x^2/(2(1-t))}.
$$

A Gaussian integral gives
$\mathbb E e^{-B_t^2/(1-t)}=\sqrt{(1-t)/(1+t)}$. Substituting
into $q_0'=\mathbb E[a_0(t,B_t)^2]$ and integrating from zero yields

$$
q_0'(t)=\frac2{\pi\sqrt{1-t^2}},\qquad
q_0(t)=\frac2\pi\arcsin t.
$$

This recovers the half-time value $1/3$. It also shows that
$q_0(t)\to1$ while $q_0'(t)\to\infty$: convergence of a function
at one does not bound its derivative there.
The constant direction $\eta=1$ is admissible and adds an atom at zero.
Its cost is

$$
D\mathcal P(0)[1]
=\frac12\int_0^1\left(\frac2\pi\arcsin t-t\right)dt
=\frac14-\frac1\pi<0.
$$

So a small positive constant coefficient improves the zero candidate.
This calculation uses the heat and variation formulas, not a minimiser
hypothesis; see also [Chen–Handschy–Lerman, proof of Theorem 6][chl-optimality].
